exam_meta.part: Part I item stem, expanded into a short-response rep

stimulus.content: Unfortunately, the last great Moghul [Mughal] ruler, Aurangzeb, opposed religious toleration. A devout Muslim and a Puritan in his habits, Aurangzeb dismissed the court musicians, artists, and historians. He discouraged poets, who "dealt in falsehood"; banned history, which "gave rise to feelings of undue pride"; and suppressed drinking and gambling. His military campaigns drained his resources. He also dismissed the Hindu clerks in his service and reimposed a poll tax on all "unbelievers." These oppressive measures against the Hindus were perhaps the most destructive acts of his reign, for memories of Aurangzeb's oppressive rule lingered in the minds of Hindu Indians for generations. By his death in 1707, the Moghul Empire was on the edge of ruin. The British came to fill the power vacuum.
stimulus.citation: Source: Donald J. Johnson et al., Through Indian Eyes, Apex Press, 1999 (adapted), from the NYS Global History and Geography II Regents Exam, June 2026

reps.exemplar: This document is from the early 1700s -- it names Aurangzeb's death in 1707 directly. It describes South Asia, specifically the Mughal Empire: the text names "the Moghul Empire" and "Hindu Indians," and mentions the British arriving afterward, which places this in the Indian subcontinent.
reps.compare_focus: Name a specific year or century and a specific region -- not "a long time ago in Asia." Then point to the exact words that told you.
compare_checklist: Did I name an approximate era (a year, a decade, or a century) rather than just 'the past'?
Did I name a specific region, not just a continent?
Did I quote or point to two details from the text itself, not the citation line?
Did I keep this to 1-3 sentences?

stimulus.content: Japanese ships are strictly forbidden to leave for foreign countries. No Japanese is permitted to go abroad. If there is anyone who attempts to do so secretly, he must be executed. The ship so involved must be impounded and its owner arrested, and the matter must be reported to the higher authority. If any Japanese returns from overseas after residing there, he must be put to death. . . . Any informer revealing the whereabouts of the followers of padres (Christians) must be rewarded accordingly. If anyone reveals the whereabouts of a high ranking padre, he must be given one hundred pieces of silver.
stimulus.citation: Source: David John Lu, Sources of Japanese History, McGraw-Hill, from the NYS Global History and Geography Regents Exam, January 2005

reps.exemplar: This is a 1635 edict, so it's from the early 1600s. It describes Japan under the Tokugawa shogunate -- the text bans Japanese people from leaving or returning, and singles out "padres" (Christian missionaries), which points to Japan's era of closing itself off from foreign contact and Christianity.
